ADVISORY_VERDICT: BANKS OPEN THE BOOKS, CHIPS TAKE THE HIT.
ADVISORY_BODY: Bank-earnings season opened this morning and it’s a real split decision. JPMorgan logged a rare quarterly miss — net income still rose 6% y/y to $15.3B and EPS +10% y/y to $5.57, but an investment-banking slowdown and a securities loss spooked the tape, and shares were down roughly 3.4% premarket. Goldman Sachs went the other way — EPS $17.01, 18.7% annualized ROE, its second-best revenue quarter ever — and Citigroup logged its best bond-trading quarter in a decade and beat profit estimates, though both are fighting a reported ‘yield-driven bank selloff’ backdrop, so a beat isn’t guaranteed to print green. Wells Fargo’s profit rose on loan growth but revenue missed, shares -1%. UnitedHealth beat clean (EPS $4.69 vs. $4.15 est.) and is +2.6% premarket; Johnson & Johnson beat adjusted EPS ($2.59 vs. $2.52 est.) and raised full-year guidance, yet still slipped -0.9% — a reminder that a good quarter doesn’t always move the stock. The bigger story is semiconductors: memory and chip names are getting dumped on fresh fears that China’s CXMT could challenge Samsung/SK Hynix/Micron, and it tore through Asia overnight — Korea’s Kospi closed -5.5% (Samsung -7.4%, SK Hynix -10.1%) — dragging Micron -3.2% and Marvell -2.6% into the U.S. premarket. Geopolitically, the Houthi-Saudi conflict is still very live (threat alerts hit Riyadh and Khamis Mushait Monday, and a tanker was struck in the Strait of Hormuz) and Iran has offered to mediate, yet oil is actually down about 2% (Brent $104.62, WTI $91.78) on hopes the Russia-Ukraine energy truce holds. CPI lands tomorrow. The Dow’s calm exterior is real, but today’s stress is sector-specific — chips and parts of financials — not systemic, at least not yet.
